newsitem.title: USA: Asarco projects growing copper surplus.
newsitem.headline: Asarco projects growing copper surplus.

text.p: Asarco Inc's latest copper supply estimate revision show growing surpluses through 1998.

The changes were disclosed early this month when chief executive Richard de J. Osborne told analysts the company was no longer projecting a supply deficit in 1997, saying it saw a Western World surplus of 60,000 short tons.

At the same time he noted the company had raised its projections of 1996 supply deficit to 43,000 tons and western demand growth to three percent without providing any of the numbers behind those estimates.
With the switch to supply surplus, Osborne projected a rise in stocks to one million tons from 940,000 this year.
But Asarco remains "confident about the outlook for refined copper market," he said, explaining it sees "a substantial inventory of excess concentrates at the end of 1997."

Company documents with the supporting data (reproduced at the end of this article) show changes in its estimates of Western World supply balance as far back as 1991, changing that year's balance to a surplus of 34,000 tons from the 138,000 ton deficit estimated last fall.
The revision boosted the estimated 1992 surplus to 362,000 tons from 96,000 and raised the 1993 surpulus to 126,000 from the 100,000 ton estimate the company used 10 months earlier.
It also boosted the company's estimates of the Western World supply deficit in 1994 to 389,000 tons from 278,000 while triming the estimated 1995 deficit to 146,000 from 308,000 tons.
There was no special reason for the July reassessment, spokesman Jerry Cooper said, pointing out the company updates its projections on a regular basis.
He said the changes had nothing to do with those being studied by the World Bureau of Metal Statistics or Sumitomo Corp's disclosure of trading irregularities.
Asarco says its figures are based on its estimates and those of the World Bureau of Metal Statistics.
"Our estimates of Western World production and consumption in 1996 and 1997 are generally not very different from other copper market analysts," Osborne told the analysts.
"We differ, however, in our estimate of East/West trade and in our analysis of the increasing difficulty of getting new mane concentrates smelted and to market."
Asarco's views of the Western World's net imports, detailed below as "West Imports" include sharp swings in China's stocks, he said.

In 1995, Asarco estimates, net imports were increased by a 95,000 ton draw-down in Chinese stocks. The company estimates the Chinese returned the 95,000 tons to stocks in 1996, cutting net west imports by that amount.
Osborne said the Chinese stock growth may be in the form of concentrates.
